cards.q: Define magnetic flux density, and state its unit.
cards.a: The force per unit current per unit length on a wire carrying a current at right angles to the field: B=FIl\displaystyle B = \frac{F}{Il}B=IlF​. Unit: the tesla, T.
cards.why: 1 T is the flux density that gives a force of 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field.

cards.q: Write the equation for the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, and state when the force is greatest and when it is zero.
cards.a: F=BIl\displaystyle F = BIlF=BIl when the wire is perpendicular to the field: this is the greatest force. The force is zero when the wire is parallel to the field.

edexcel.note: Edexcel writes the general case as F=BIlsin⁡θ\displaystyle F = BIl\sin\thetaF=BIlsinθ, where θ\displaystyle \thetaθ is the angle between the wire and the field.

cards.q: A wire of length 0.050 m carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on it.
cards.a: 0.030 N
steps: F=BIl=0.20×3.0×0.050\displaystyle F = BIl = 0.20 \times 3.0 \times 0.050F=BIl=0.20×3.0×0.050
F=0.030 N\displaystyle F = 0.030\ \text{N}F=0.030 N

cards.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does each of the thumb, first finger and second finger represent?
cards.a: Thumb: the force (motion). First finger: the field, north to south. Second finger: the conventional current, positive to negative.

cards.q: Outline how to use a top-pan balance to investigate how the force on a wire in a magnetic field depends on the current.
cards.a: Rest the magnets on the balance, clamp the wire between them, and record the change in reading for each current.
marks: Place a pair of magnets on a yoke on a top-pan balance, and clamp a straight wire in the field between them, at right angles to the field.
Zero the balance with no current.
Pass a current through the wire, measured with an ammeter, and record the balance reading.
The force on the wire equals the change in reading × g\displaystyle gg: by Newton's third law the magnets feel an equal and opposite force.
Repeat for a range of currents and plot force against current: a straight line through the origin, with gradient Bl\displaystyle BlBl.

cards.q: Write the equation for the force on a charged particle moving at right angles to a magnetic field.
cards.a: F=BQv\displaystyle F = BQvF=BQv

edexcel.note: Edexcel writes the general case as F=Bqvsin⁡θ\displaystyle F = Bqv\sin\thetaF=Bqvsinθ.

cards.q: An electron moves at 2.0×106 m s−1\displaystyle 2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}2.0×106 m s−1 at right angles to a field of flux density 0.010 T. Calculate the force on it. (e=1.60×10−19 C\displaystyle e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}e=1.60×10−19 C)
cards.a: 3.2×10−15 N\displaystyle 3.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{N}3.2×10−15 N
steps: F=BQv=0.010×1.60×10−19×2.0×106\displaystyle F = BQv = 0.010 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6}F=BQv=0.010×1.60×10−19×2.0×106
F=3.2×10−15 N\displaystyle F = 3.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{N}F=3.2×10−15 N

cards.q: When using Fleming's left-hand rule for a moving electron, which way should the second finger point?
cards.a: Opposite to the electron's direction of motion. The second finger shows conventional current, which is the direction a positive charge would move.

cards.q: Explain why a charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field follows a circular path at constant speed.
cards.a: The magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity.
marks: The force on the particle is always perpendicular to its velocity.
A force perpendicular to the velocity changes the direction of motion but not the speed: it does no work.
The force has constant magnitude and always points towards the same centre, so it acts as a centripetal force.
The particle therefore moves in a circle at constant speed.

cards.q: Derive an expression for the radius of the circular path of a particle of mass m\displaystyle mm and charge Q\displaystyle QQ moving at speed v\displaystyle vv at right angles to a field B\displaystyle BB.
cards.a: r=mvBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{mv}{BQ}r=BQmv​
cards.why: Faster or heavier particles curve less; a stronger field or a larger charge curves them more.
steps: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: BQv=mv2r\displaystyle BQv = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}BQv=rmv2​.
Cancel one v\displaystyle vv and rearrange: r=mvBQ\displaystyle r = \frac{mv}{BQ}r=BQmv​.

cards.q: In a cyclotron, how does the time for one orbit depend on the particle's speed?
cards.a: It does not. T=2πmBQ\displaystyle T = \frac{2\pi m}{BQ}T=BQ2πm​: faster particles move in larger circles and take the same time per orbit.
cards.why: This is why an alternating potential difference of fixed frequency can accelerate the particles every time they cross the gap.

cards.q: Define magnetic flux, and state its unit.
cards.a: The product of the flux density and the area it passes through at right angles: Φ=BA\displaystyle \Phi = BAΦ=BA. Unit: the weber, Wb.

cards.q: What is magnetic flux linkage?
cards.a: The flux through a coil multiplied by its number of turns: NΦ\displaystyle N\PhiNΦ.

cards.q: A coil of N\displaystyle NN turns and area A\displaystyle AA is in a field B\displaystyle BB. Write its flux linkage when the normal to the coil makes an angle θ\displaystyle \thetaθ with the field.
cards.a: NΦ=BANcos⁡θ\displaystyle N\Phi = BAN\cos\thetaNΦ=BANcosθ
cards.why: The flux linkage is greatest when the plane of the coil is at right angles to the field (θ=0\displaystyle \theta = 0θ=0), and zero when the coil is edge-on to it.

cards.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0×10−3 m2\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{2}4.0×10−3 m2 lies with its plane at right angles to a field of flux density 0.050 T. Calculate the flux linkage.
cards.a: 0.040 Wb
steps: NΦ=BAN=0.050×4.0×10−3×200\displaystyle N\Phi = BAN = 0.050 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 200NΦ=BAN=0.050×4.0×10−3×200
NΦ=0.040 Wb\displaystyle N\Phi = 0.040\ \text{Wb}NΦ=0.040 Wb

cards.q: Outline how to use a search coil and an oscilloscope to investigate how flux linkage depends on the angle between the coil and the field.
cards.a: Put the search coil in an alternating magnetic field and measure the induced emf at each angle.
marks: Produce an alternating magnetic field with a large coil connected to an alternating supply.
Place a small search coil at the centre of the field, connected to an oscilloscope.
The peak emf shown on the oscilloscope is proportional to the flux linkage through the search coil.
Turn the search coil through measured angles and record the peak emf at each.
Plot peak emf against cos⁡θ\displaystyle \cos\thetacosθ: a straight line through the origin.

cards.q: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
cards.a: The magnitude of the induced emf is equal to the rate of change of flux linkage.

cards.q: State Lenz's law.
cards.a: The direction of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change that produces it.

cards.q: Write the equation that combines Faraday's and Lenz's laws, and say what the minus sign represents.
cards.a: ε=−NΔΦΔt\displaystyle \varepsilon = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}ε=−NΔtΔΦ​. The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced emf opposes the change in flux linkage.

cards.q: The flux linkage through a coil falls from 0.040 Wb to zero in 0.020 s. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf.
cards.a: 2.0 V
steps: ε=Δ(NΦ)Δt=0.0400.020\displaystyle \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t} = \frac{0.040}{0.020}ε=ΔtΔ(NΦ)​=0.0200.040​
ε=2.0 V\displaystyle \varepsilon = 2.0\ \text{V}ε=2.0 V

cards.q: Explain how Lenz's law follows from the conservation of energy, for a magnet pushed into a coil.
cards.a: If the induced current helped the motion, energy would appear from nothing.
marks: The induced current makes the coil a magnet, with a pole facing the incoming magnet.
By Lenz's law that pole repels the magnet, so work must be done to push the magnet in.
This work is the source of the electrical energy in the coil.
If the coil attracted the magnet instead, the magnet would accelerate and electrical energy would be produced with no work done, which would violate conservation of energy.

cards.q: A magnet is moved into a coil. State three ways of increasing the emf induced.
cards.a: Move the magnet faster, use a stronger magnet, or use a coil with more turns.
cards.why: Each increases the rate of change of flux linkage.

cards.q: Explain why an emf is induced in a coil when the current in a neighbouring coil is changed.
cards.a: The changing current changes the flux linking the second coil.
cards.why: A steady current induces nothing: there must be a change.
marks: The current in the first coil produces a magnetic field, whose flux passes through the second coil.
Changing the current changes this magnetic flux.
The flux linkage of the second coil therefore changes.
By Faraday's law an emf is induced in the second coil, equal to the rate of change of its flux linkage.

cards.q: A straight conductor of length 0.10 m moves at 5.0 m s−1\displaystyle 5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}5.0 m s−1 at right angles to a field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the emf induced across its ends.
cards.a: 0.10 V
steps: Each second the conductor sweeps out an area lv\displaystyle lvlv, cutting flux Blv\displaystyle BlvBlv.
ε=Blv=0.20×0.10×5.0\displaystyle \varepsilon = Blv = 0.20 \times 0.10 \times 5.0ε=Blv=0.20×0.10×5.0
ε=0.10 V\displaystyle \varepsilon = 0.10\ \text{V}ε=0.10 V

cards.q: Write the equation for the emf induced in a coil rotating at angular speed ω\displaystyle \omegaω in a uniform magnetic field. What is its peak value?
cards.a: ε=BANωsin⁡ωt\displaystyle \varepsilon = BAN\omega\sin\omega tε=BANωsinωt. The peak emf is BANω\displaystyle BAN\omegaBANω.

cards.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0×10−3 m2\displaystyle 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{2}4.0×10−3 m2 rotates at 100 rad s−1\displaystyle 100\ \text{rad s}^{-1}100 rad s−1 in a field of 0.050 T. Calculate the peak emf.
cards.a: 4.0 V
steps: εmax=BANω=0.050×4.0×10−3×200×100\displaystyle \varepsilon_{\text{max}} = BAN\omega = 0.050 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 200 \times 100εmax​=BANω=0.050×4.0×10−3×200×100
εmax=4.0 V\displaystyle \varepsilon_{\text{max}} = 4.0\ \text{V}εmax​=4.0 V

cards.q: For a coil rotating in a magnetic field, where is the coil when the induced emf is greatest, and what is its flux linkage then?
cards.a: When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field. The flux linkage is then zero, but it is changing at its fastest rate.
cards.why: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage, not on its size.

cards.q: What is the root mean square (rms) value of an alternating current?
cards.a: The value of the steady direct current that would deliver the same power to a resistor.

cards.q: Write the equations linking the rms values of a sinusoidal current and potential difference to their peak values.
cards.a: Irms=I02\displaystyle I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}Irms​=2​I0​​ and Vrms=V02\displaystyle V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}Vrms​=2​V0​​

cards.q: The mains supply has an rms potential difference of 230 V. Calculate its peak value.
cards.a: 325 V
cards.why: The peak-to-peak value is twice this: 650 V.
steps: V0=2×Vrms=2×230\displaystyle V_{0} = \sqrt{2} \times V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{2} \times 230V0​=2​×Vrms​=2​×230
V0=325 V\displaystyle V_{0} = 325\ \text{V}V0​=325 V

cards.q: For an alternating potential difference, what is the difference between the peak value and the peak-to-peak value?
cards.a: The peak value is the maximum, measured from zero. The peak-to-peak value is from the highest point to the lowest: twice the peak value.

cards.q: On an oscilloscope, one complete cycle of an alternating signal covers 4.0 divisions. The time base is 5.0 ms per division. Calculate the frequency.
cards.a: 50 Hz
steps: Period: T=4.0×5.0 ms=20 ms=0.020 s\displaystyle T = 4.0 \times 5.0\ \text{ms} = 20\ \text{ms} = 0.020\ \text{s}T=4.0×5.0 ms=20 ms=0.020 s.
f=1T=10.020\displaystyle f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{0.020}f=T1​=0.0201​
f=50 Hz\displaystyle f = 50\ \text{Hz}f=50 Hz

cards.q: How is the peak potential difference of an alternating signal read from an oscilloscope?
cards.a: Measure the peak-to-peak height of the trace in divisions, multiply by the Y-gain (volts per division), and halve it.
cards.why: Measuring peak to peak and halving is more precise than judging where zero is.

cards.q: Write the transformer equation linking the numbers of turns to the potential differences.
cards.a: NsNp=VsVp\displaystyle \frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = \frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}Np​Ns​​=Vp​Vs​​

cards.q: A transformer steps 230 V down to 12 V. Its primary coil has 1150 turns. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
cards.a: 60 turns
steps: Ns=Np×VsVp=1150×12230\displaystyle N_{s} = N_{p} \times \frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = 1150 \times \frac{12}{230}Ns​=Np​×Vp​Vs​​=1150×23012​
Ns=60\displaystyle N_{s} = 60Ns​=60

cards.q: Write the equation for the efficiency of a transformer.
cards.a: efficiency=IsVsIpVp\displaystyle \text{efficiency} = \frac{I_{s}V_{s}}{I_{p}V_{p}}efficiency=Ip​Vp​Is​Vs​​

cards.q: What are eddy currents in a transformer core, and how are they reduced?
cards.a: Currents induced in the iron core by the changing magnetic flux, which heat the core and waste energy. They are reduced by making the core from thin laminations insulated from one another.

cards.q: State four causes of inefficiency in a transformer.
cards.a: Heating, eddy currents, magnetising the core, and flux that misses the secondary coil.
marks: Heating of the coils by the current, because the wires have resistance.
Eddy currents induced in the core.
Energy needed to magnetise and demagnetise the core repeatedly.
Flux leakage: not all the flux from the primary passes through the secondary.

cards.q: Explain why electrical power is transmitted at high voltage.
cards.a: For the same power, a higher voltage means a smaller current and far less heating of the cables.
marks: For a given power, P=IV\displaystyle P = IVP=IV, so a higher voltage means a smaller current.
The power wasted heating the cables is I2R\displaystyle I^{2}RI2R.
A smaller current greatly reduces this loss, because it depends on the current squared.

cards.q: A power station sends 1.0 MW along a cable of resistance 10 Ω at 25 kV. Calculate the power lost in the cable.
cards.a: 1.6×104 W\displaystyle 1.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}1.6×104 W
cards.why: Do not use V2R\displaystyle \frac{V^{2}}{R}RV2​ with 25 kV: that is not the potential difference across the cable.
steps: Current in the cable: I=PV=1.0×10625×103=40 A\displaystyle I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{6}}{25 \times 10^{3}} = 40\ \text{A}I=VP​=25×1031.0×106​=40 A.
Power lost: I2R=402×10\displaystyle I^{2}R = 40^{2} \times 10I2R=402×10
=1.6×104 W\displaystyle = 1.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}=1.6×104 W
